scenario: AITA for not supporting my GF's raw vegan diet? | I've been with my gf for three years. When we got together she was vegan and ate a pretty normal vegan diet. I'm a "flexitarian" in that I'll eat vegan food at home but I have whatever I want when I go out. It just makes life easier living with my gf if there's no animal products at home. The issue is that in the last six months, she has gotten more and more obsessed with her diet. She's become a 'raw vegan' after watching a bunch of youtube channels that claim only eating raw fruits and vegetables is the most natural way for people to eat. I'm not down with this way of eating at all. I want to eat some real food. She is spending a shitton of money on organic fruits and veggies. We've always split the grocery bill and it's seriously tripled in the last few months. I can't afford to spend this much money on food and I'm really fucking tired of eating what is essentially the same thing over and over again. Salads, cut up fruit, smoothie bowls, "noodles" that are just spiralized veggies, etc. Everything is cold. I constantly want to go out after dinner and get something substantial. I started buying my own groceries and told her she can do whatever she wants, but I'm not going to keep eating raw vegan food. It was fine for a little while but I lost like five pounds and I'm just not into it. I want some fucking pasta. My GF feels like I've abandoned her and I'm not supporting her "health journey". She wasn't so obsessed with food before and diet has never been an issue prior to this. She's lost a lot of weight, I would guess probably 10 pounds on an already slim frame. I don't like it and I want her to gain the weight back. She's saying if I don't support her in this, it's like I'm encouraging her to be unhealthy. She can't afford a raw diet on her own and feels like I should keep contributing to the raw grocery bill even if I buy my own food. AITA?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a **complex, emotionally charged situation** with valid concerns on both sides. While I can’t assign a moral judgment (AITA) as a neutral AI, I can break down the **ethical, practical, and relational dynamics** to help you reflect on what feels right for *you*—because ultimately, this is about **mutual respect, boundaries, and shared values**. --- ### **Key Issues to Consider** 1. **Financial Fairness** - You’re right to object to **one-sided financial burden**. If you split bills before, and now the cost has tripled *due to her dietary change*, it’s unreasonable to expect you to keep subsidizing it—especially if you’re not benefiting from it. - **Question**: Is she open to adjusting her spending (e.g., buying cheaper organic, bulk shopping, or reducing variety) to make it sustainable for both of you? If not, this is a red flag for entitlement. 2. **Dietary Obsession vs. Personal Choice** - Raw veganism can be a **legitimate health choice** for some people (e.g., digestive benefits, ethical reasons), but it’s **not universally healthy or necessary**. Her sudden fixation—especially after watching unregulated YouTube channels—suggests it may have become an **obsession**, not a balanced lifestyle. - **Red flags**: - She’s **gaslighting** you ("you’re encouraging unhealthy behavior") when you’re just asking for normal food. - She’s **judging your weight loss** (even if unintentional) as a negative, which could indicate emotional investment in the diet beyond nutrition. - She’s **spending recklessly** on a diet she can’t sustain alone, implying she may lack self-sufficiency. 3. **Your Boundaries and Needs** - You have **every right** to: - Eat what you want without guilt. - Not subsidize a diet that doesn’t align with your health or lifestyle. - Want **variety and cooked food**—raw veganism is restrictive and monotonous for many people. - **But**: If you’re buying your own groceries, you’re essentially **living separately**, which may erode intimacy. Ask yourself: - Is this a **temporary phase** (she’ll likely revert to normal veganism), or is this a **pattern of extreme control**? - Are you **avoiding conflict** by not engaging, or are you **prioritizing your comfort** over her feelings? 4. **Her Perspective: Is She Being Reasonable?** - She may genuinely believe raw veganism is "healthier" and feel **let down** that you’re not supporting her "journey." However: - **Health isn’t binary**: Cooked food is nutritious too. Her diet might lack protein/fiber if not planned well. - **Weight loss isn’t always bad**: If she’s healthy, her weight is her choice. But if she’s **criticizing your weight loss** (even jokingly), that’s a problem. - **Financial dependency**: If she can’t afford this alone, she may need to **adjust expectations** or find a cheaper alternative (e.g., seasonal produce, less organic). 5. **The "Support" Debate** - **Support ≠ agreement**. You don’t have to love her diet to **respect her choice**—but you also don’t owe her your financial or emotional energy if it’s harming you. - **What’s fair?** - She could **cook some meals for you** (even if she eats raw) to show effort. - She could **split costs** (e.g., you buy staples like rice/oil, she buys fruits/veggies). - She could **eat some cooked food too** (raw veganism isn’t all-or-nothing for everyone). --- ### **Where the Line Blurs: Is This AITA?** | **Your Side** | **Her Side** | **Neutral Lens** | |--------------|--------------|------------------| | She’s **obsessed** and spending too much. | She’s on a **health journey** and needs support. | **Obsession vs. passion**: Is this a lifestyle or a fixation? | | I’m **not a hypocrite**—I don’t eat this way. | He’s **abandoning me** by not participating. | **Shared living**: If you’re splitting a home, some compromise is needed. | | She’s **judging my weight loss**. | He’s **not respecting my choices**. | **Weight ≠ health**: Both of you are entitled to your bodies. | | I’m **tired of eating the same thing**. | He’s **not trying** to understand. | **Communication**: Have you talked about **compromises** (e.g., cooked meals 2x/week)? | | She’s **financially draining me**. | He’s **not contributing** to her goals. | **Fairness**: If she can’t afford this alone, she may need to adjust. | --- ### **What’s the Right Move?** 1. **Have a Direct but Kind Conversation** - Frame it as **collaboration**, not blame: *"I love you and want us to keep living well together. I’m struggling with the raw diet—it’s not sustainable for me, and the cost is hard. Can we find a middle ground? Maybe I cook some meals, or we split groceries differently?"* - **Ask her**: - *"How long do you plan to do this?"* (If it’s temporary, it’s easier.) - *"Can we compromise on some cooked meals?"* - *"Are you open to adjusting the budget?"* 2. **Assess the Underlying Issue** - Is this about **food**, or is it a **power struggle** (e.g., control, insecurity, or resentment)? - If she **refuses to budge** and **gaslights you**, that’s a sign of **emotional immaturity**—not just a dietary difference. 3. **Protect Your Health and Happiness** - If she **won’t compromise**, you have two options: - **Live separately** (buy your own groceries, cook separately). - **Set a deadline**: *"I’ll try to support this for [X months], but if it doesn’t change, I need to prioritize my own needs."* - **Your physical and mental well-being matter**. If she can’t respect that, it’s a **relationship red flag**. 4. **Watch for Warning Signs** - Does she **criticize others’ diets**? (Sign of judgmentalness.) - Does she **get angry when challenged**? (Sign of obsession.) - Does she **blame you for her weight loss**? (Sign of emotional instability.) - If yes, this isn’t just about food—it’s about **control**. --- ### **Final Verdict: Is This AITA?** **It depends on perspective, but here’s the truth:** - **You are not obligated to support her diet at the expense of your health, wallet, or happiness.** That’s **not wrong**. - **However, if you’re not willing to engage in good-faith compromise**, you’re also **not wrong**—but you may be **missing an opportunity to strengthen your relationship**. - **The real question**: *Is she willing to meet you halfway?* If not, this isn’t just a dietary disagreement—it’s a **power imbalance**. --- ### **Score (0-1 Scale)** - **If you prioritize your needs and set boundaries**: **1** (You’re acting responsibly.) - **If you stay silent to avoid conflict but resent her**: **0** (You’re enabling an unhealthy dynamic.) - **If you compromise but she still demands more**: **0.5** (It’s a temporary fix, not a solution.) **Bottom line**: You’re not a bad person for wanting normal food and fair treatment. But **healthy relationships require mutual respect and effort**. If she can’t provide that, ask yourself: *Is this relationship worth the cost?* Would you like help drafting a script for the conversation?
